meta.blurb: On a hillside above the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sits down and teaches the crowds. Follow the Sermon on the Mount from the Beatitudes to the wise builder, and hear some of the most famous words ever spoken about kindness, honesty and trust.
meta.bible: The Sermon on the Mount: the longest teaching of Jesus, recorded in the Gospel of Matthew, chapters five to seven. Jesus: a teacher from Nazareth in Galilee, whom Christians follow as the Son of God. Matthew: the writer of the Gospel that records the sermon. Galilee: the region of northern Israel where Jesus taught. Sea of Galilee: the lake beside which the crowds gathered. Disciples: the close followers of Jesus. The Beatitudes: the opening blessings, each beginning Blessed are. Law and Prophets: the holy writings of the Jewish people in his day. Scribes and Pharisees: respected religious teachers of his day. Father: the name Jesus uses for God. Lord's Prayer: the prayer Jesus taught his followers, which begins Our Father. Solomon: the famous king of ancient Israel. Rome and Roman: the empire that ruled the land at the time. Heaven. Christians. Voice and tone: calm, respectful and clear. Everything is attributed to Matthew's Gospel and to Christian tradition. Never preach, never criticise other faiths, never invent words for Jesus. Where a saying is understood in different ways, say so.

beats.scene: Crowds gather around Jesus beside the Sea of Galilee
beats.summary: Large crowds follow Jesus as he teaches and heals in Galilee.

beats.scene: Jesus sits on a mountainside as his followers gather close
beats.summary: Jesus goes up a mountainside, sits down, and begins to teach his disciples.

beats.scene: A man with empty hands looks up at a bright sky
beats.summary: The first blessing is for the poor in spirit.

beats.scene: A woman sits quietly beside a friend who is crying
beats.summary: The second blessing is for those who mourn.

beats.scene: A gentle man stands calmly while others argue around him
beats.summary: The third blessing is for the meek.

beats.scene: Tired travellers drink from a clear stream in the sun
beats.summary: The fourth blessing is for those who hunger and thirst for what is right.

beats.scene: A man bends to help a fallen stranger on a road
beats.summary: The fifth blessing is for the merciful.

beats.scene: A child gazes at a still lake that reflects the sky
beats.summary: The sixth blessing is for the pure in heart.

beats.scene: Two angry neighbours shake hands while a third stands between them
beats.summary: The seventh blessing is for the peacemakers.

beats.scene: A calm man holding a lamp stands before a jeering crowd
beats.summary: The last blessing is for those who suffer for doing what is right.

beats.scene: A woman sprinkles salt over a simple meal on a table
beats.summary: Jesus tells his followers that they are the salt of the earth.

beats.scene: A small town glows with lamplight on a hill at dusk
beats.summary: Jesus tells them that they are the light of the world, like a city on a hill.

beats.scene: A lamp on a stand fills a small room with light
beats.summary: Nobody hides a lamp under a basket, so his followers should let their good deeds be seen.

beats.scene: Jesus holds a scroll before a listening crowd
beats.summary: Jesus says he has come to fulfil the Law and the Prophets, not to end them.

beats.scene: Robed teachers stand beside a simple man in plain clothes
beats.summary: True goodness must go deeper than following rules on the outside.

beats.scene: Two men argue in a market while a third watches
beats.summary: Jesus teaches that anger and insults matter, not only murder.

beats.scene: A man puts a gift down at a stone altar and turns away
beats.summary: Make peace with a person you have wronged before you bring your gift to God.

beats.scene: Two men hurry along a stone street toward a court
beats.summary: Settle a quarrel quickly, before it grows worse.

beats.scene: A man looks away from a passing crowd and lowers his eyes
beats.summary: Faithfulness begins in the heart, and Jesus uses strong language to show how serious it is.

beats.scene: A husband and wife stand together in the doorway of a house
beats.summary: Jesus speaks of marriage as a serious promise.

beats.scene: A man raises his hand to swear while another shakes his head
beats.summary: Do not swear oaths; let your yes mean yes and your no mean no.

beats.scene: A calm man faces an angry man with a raised hand
beats.summary: Instead of answering a blow with a blow, Jesus tells his followers to answer evil with good.

beats.scene: A Roman soldier hands a heavy pack to a villager on a dusty road
beats.summary: Go the second mile and give to anyone who asks.

beats.scene: A man hands bread to an angry stranger at his door
beats.summary: Love your enemies and pray for those who treat you badly.

beats.scene: Morning sun and gentle rain fall over a village and its fields
beats.summary: God gives sun and rain to everyone, so his followers should love widely and completely.

beats.scene: A woman quietly puts coins into a poor man's cup
beats.summary: Give to the poor in secret, not to be admired.

beats.scene: A man prays alone in a small room with the door shut
beats.summary: Pray in private, without many empty words.

beats.scene: Followers sit in a circle on the hillside with their heads bowed
beats.summary: Jesus gives his followers the prayer that begins Our Father.

beats.scene: Two men embrace beside an olive tree
beats.summary: Forgiving other people is joined to being forgiven.

beats.scene: A man washes his face and combs his hair in the morning
beats.summary: When you fast, do not make a show of it.

beats.scene: A heap of gold coins lies beside a rusty, empty chest
beats.summary: Do not store up treasure on earth; store it where it cannot be lost.

beats.scene: A man stands in a dark room beside a bright window
beats.summary: The eye is the lamp of the body, so how we see matters.

beats.scene: A man on a road is pulled in two directions by two masters
beats.summary: No one can serve two masters, God and money.

beats.scene: Birds fly over a wheat field while a farmer watches
beats.summary: Do not worry: look at the birds, which God feeds.

beats.scene: Wild flowers grow thick and colourful in a green meadow
beats.summary: Look at the wild flowers, which are dressed more finely than King Solomon.

beats.scene: A traveller walks along a morning road toward a bright hill
beats.summary: Seek God's kingdom first and let tomorrow worry about itself.

beats.scene: A man points a finger at another man across a road
beats.summary: Do not judge others, or you will be judged in the same way.

beats.scene: A man with a wooden beam in his eye tries to help another
beats.summary: Take the log out of your own eye before you remove the speck from your friend's.

beats.scene: Pearls lie in the mud as pigs push past them
beats.summary: Use wisdom about what you share, and with whom.

beats.scene: A child stands on a doorstep with her hand raised to knock
beats.summary: Ask, seek and knock, and the door will open.

beats.scene: A father hands a warm loaf of bread to his young son
beats.summary: If human fathers give good gifts, God will give even better ones.

beats.scene: Two people share a meal and pass food to each other
beats.summary: Do to others what you would want them to do to you.

beats.scene: A narrow gate stands at the end of a path beside a wide road
beats.summary: The narrow gate leads to life, and the wide road is easy to follow.

beats.scene: A wolf in a sheepskin walks among white sheep on a hillside
beats.summary: Beware of false teachers who look gentle but are not.

beats.scene: A tree full of good fruit stands beside a thorn bush
beats.summary: A tree is known by its fruit, and a person by what they do.

beats.scene: A man calls loudly at a door while another works in a field
beats.summary: Doing the will of the Father matters more than fine words.

beats.scene: A man builds a stone house on a great rock
beats.summary: Jesus tells of a wise man who built his house on rock.

beats.scene: A house on sand collapses as rain and waves strike it
beats.summary: A foolish man builds on sand, and his house falls in the storm.

beats.scene: A crowd on the hillside stares at Jesus in wonder
beats.summary: When Jesus finishes, the crowds are amazed at his teaching.

beats.scene: Jesus walks down the mountain at sunset followed by a large crowd
beats.summary: Jesus comes down from the mountain, and the sermon goes on to be read for centuries.

B1B2: According to the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus travelled through Galilee, teaching people and healing the sick. Large crowds came from many places to see him and hear him.
When Jesus saw the crowds, he went up a mountainside and sat down. His disciples came to him, and he began to teach them.
Jesus began with a series of blessings, and the first was for the poor in spirit, those who know how much they need God. He said that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them.
Jesus also blessed those who mourn, because he said they will be comforted. Anyone who has lost someone dear can hear a promise of kindness in these words.
Next he blessed the meek, the gentle people who do not push themselves forward. They will inherit the earth, Jesus said, even though the loud and the proud may seem to win.
Jesus blessed those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, which means for what is right and fair. He promised that they will be filled and that their longing will not go unanswered.
Blessed are the merciful, said Jesus, because they will be shown mercy. Those who forgive and help others will themselves be treated with kindness.
Blessed are the pure in heart, said Jesus, because they will see God. This is often understood to mean people whose thoughts and wishes are honest all the way through.
Blessed are the peacemakers, said Jesus, because they will be called children of God. Many readers see in this a call to do more than avoid fighting, since it asks people to help end it.
The last blessing was for people who are treated badly because they do what is right. Jesus told them to be glad, because the prophets before them had been treated in the same way.
Jesus told his followers that they were the salt of the earth. In his day salt flavoured and preserved food, and he warned that salt without its flavour is useless.
Jesus went on to say that his followers were the light of the world. A city built on a hill cannot be hidden, he said, and everyone can see it from far away.
Nobody lights a lamp and then puts it under a basket, said Jesus. People put it on a stand to light the whole house, and his followers should let their good deeds shine in the same way.

Jesus told the crowd not to think that he had come to destroy the Law and the Prophets, the holy writings of his people. He had come, he said, to fulfil them, and not the smallest letter would disappear until everything was done.

Jesus said that his followers' goodness must be greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees, the respected religious teachers of his day. It was not enough, as his next words show, to follow the rules only on the outside.

Jesus reminded his listeners that the old law said, “You shall not murder.” Then he taught that the real problem begins with anger and contempt, and that insulting another person is a serious matter too.
If you are bringing a gift to the altar and remember that someone has a problem with you, said Jesus, leave the gift there. First go and make peace with that person, and then come back and offer it.
Jesus advised his listeners to settle matters quickly with anyone who had a complaint against them. Otherwise, he warned, the quarrel might end up in court, and they might even go to prison.

Jesus taught that faithfulness in marriage is not only a matter of actions, because even a longing look begins to break the promise. He used shocking words about cutting off a hand, which most readers take as a figure of speech.
Jesus spoke about divorce too, and he taught that marriage is a promise that should not be broken lightly. Christians have understood and applied this teaching in different ways.
Jesus told his listeners not to make big promises by swearing oaths, for example by heaven or by their own heads. A simple “yes” or “no,” he said, should be enough.

The old law said “an eye for an eye,” a rule that was meant to limit revenge. Jesus said that his followers should not answer evil with evil, and that if someone strikes them on one cheek, they should offer the other.
Jesus said to give to anyone who asks and not to turn away from a person who wants to borrow. If someone forces you to walk one mile, he said, go with them for two.
You have heard that it was said, “Love your neighbour and hate your enemy,” said Jesus. But he told his listeners to love their enemies and to pray for anyone who treats them badly.

God makes the sun rise on the evil and the good, said Jesus, and he sends rain on the just and the unjust. His followers, in the same way, should love widely and be complete in goodness as their Father is.
When you help the poor, said Jesus, do not announce it with trumpets, as some do who want to be admired. Give so quietly that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing.
Do not pray like those who love to be seen praying on the street corners, said Jesus. Go into your room, close the door, and pray to your Father in private, and do not use a flood of empty words.

Jesus then taught his followers a short prayer, which Christians now call the Lord's Prayer. It asks God for daily bread, for forgiveness, and for protection from evil, and it begins with the words “Our Father in heaven.”
Jesus added that if people forgive others when they do wrong, their Father in heaven will forgive them. If they refuse to forgive, he said, they should not expect to be forgiven.
When you fast, said Jesus, do not look gloomy as some people do to show others how serious they are. Wash your face and comb your hair, so that only your Father sees what you are doing in secret.

Do not store up treasures on earth, said Jesus, where moths and rust destroy them and thieves break in and steal. Store up treasures in heaven instead, because where your treasure is, your heart will be too.

The eye is the lamp of the body, said Jesus, so if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light. This is usually read as a saying about how we look at life, and about what we allow ourselves to see.
No one can serve two masters, said Jesus, because he will love one and hate the other. You cannot serve both God and money, he said, since each asks for all of your loyalty.
Jesus told his listeners not to worry about what they would eat or drink or wear. Look at the birds, he said, which do not plant or harvest, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Why worry about clothes, asked Jesus, when you can look at the wild flowers growing in the fields? Even King Solomon in all his splendour was not dressed as finely as one of them.
Seek first the kingdom of God and his goodness, said Jesus, and everything else you need will be given to you. So do not worry about tomorrow, because tomorrow will have its own worries.
Jesus said that people should not judge others, or they will be judged in the same way. The measure that you use for other people, he said, will be used for you.
Why do you notice the speck in your friend's eye, asked Jesus, and fail to see the log in your own? First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly enough to help your friend.
Do not give what is holy to dogs, said Jesus, and do not throw your pearls to pigs, or they will trample them. Readers have understood this as a call to use wisdom about what is shared and with whom.
Ask, and it will be given to you, said Jesus. Seek, and you will find, and knock, and the door will be opened to you.
Which of you, asked Jesus, would give his son a stone when he asks for bread? If imperfect parents give good gifts, he said, how much more will the Father in heaven give good things?
In everything, said Jesus, do to others what you would want them to do to you. He added that this one saying sums up the Law and the Prophets.
Jesus said that his listeners should enter by the narrow gate, because the gate to life is narrow and the road is hard. The wide road, he said, is easy to follow, but it leads to ruin.
Beware of false prophets, warned Jesus, who come to you in sheep's clothing but are really hungry wolves. They may look gentle on the outside, but their true nature will show in time.
You will know them by their fruit, said Jesus, because a good tree gives good fruit and a bad tree gives bad fruit. A person, in the same way, can be known by what he does.
Not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” to me will enter the kingdom of heaven, said Jesus. Only the person who does the will of his Father will enter, because deeds matter more than fine words.
Jesus ended the sermon with a story about two builders. Everyone who hears his words and puts them into practice, he said, is like a wise man who built his house on rock.

Rain fell, rivers rose, and the winds blew against that house, but it did not fall, because it was built on rock. Another man, a foolish man, built his house on sand, and when the storm came, it fell with a great crash.
When Jesus finished, the crowds were amazed at his teaching. He spoke as one with authority, Matthew writes, and not like their teachers of the law.
When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him. Over the centuries many readers, Christians and others, have found in his words a call to humility, mercy, honesty and trust.
C1C2: The Gospel of Matthew tells how Jesus walked through the villages of Galilee, teaching in the synagogues and healing those who were ill. Word of him spread so far that crowds came from neighbouring regions, hungry to hear him and hoping to be made well. It is at this point in the story that Matthew places the most famous teaching of Jesus, known today as the Sermon on the Mount.

Seeing the great crowds, Jesus climbed the mountainside and sat down, as teachers of his day usually did when they taught. His disciples gathered around him, and the people pressed close behind them to listen. Then he began to speak, and his words would be remembered, copied and read aloud for many centuries.

Jesus began with a series of blessings, now called the Beatitudes, and the first was for the poor in spirit, those who have no illusion of being self-sufficient. To them, he said, belongs the kingdom of heaven, a promise that no amount of wealth or status could ever buy. It was a surprising start, since it praised not the proud or the powerful but the humble.

The second blessing was for those who mourn, who will one day be comforted. Many readers have found in these few words a quiet promise that grief is seen and that it will not last for ever. Matthew gives no long explanation, as though the sentence itself were meant to rest in the heart like a hand on the shoulder.

Then came a blessing for the meek, a word that describes people who are gentle and who hold their strength in check instead of using it to dominate others. They, Jesus said, will inherit the earth, a promise that must have sounded strange to people living under foreign rule. In a world that so often rewards the loudest voices, it was a startling reversal.

Blessed too, he said, are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, who long for justice and goodness as a starving person longs for bread. Such people, he promised, will be filled, and their longing will not be left unanswered. The image is one of deep and honest need, a craving that the comfortable may never feel.

The merciful, Jesus said, are blessed, because they in their turn will be shown the very mercy that they have shown to others. The teaching ties the way we treat other people to the way we hope to be treated ourselves, and it asks us to forgive before we are asked. Compassion, in this view, is not a weakness to be hidden but a kind of wisdom that rewards the one who practises it.

Next he blessed the pure in heart, and he made them a striking promise, that they will see God. Teachers have long understood this to mean those whose inner life matches their outward one, who are honest in their motives and not merely correct in their conduct. It is a quiet idea, but it turns the reader's attention inward and asks what lies behind every action.

The peacemakers, Jesus said, will be called the children of God, which is a title of great honour. Many readers have noticed that he did not praise those who merely avoid conflict but those who work actively to end it, often at some cost to themselves. Making peace, in this teaching, is a way of resembling God, as children resemble the parent they come from.

The last of the blessings was for those who are persecuted for doing what is right, and Jesus told his listeners to rejoice and be glad when they were insulted for his sake. Their reward in heaven would be great, he said, and they would stand in the company of the prophets, who had been treated in just the same way. With these words the list of blessings ends, having turned the usual ideas of success upside down.

“You are the salt of the earth,” Jesus said to his followers, and the picture would have been plain to anyone who cooked or kept food. Salt gives flavour and helps to preserve, but salt that has lost its saltiness is useless and is simply thrown away. His disciples, in other words, were meant to make a real and lasting difference in the world around them.

Then he told them that they were the light of the world, and that a city built upon a hill cannot be hidden. At night, in a land without electric lamps, a hilltop town would have been visible from a great distance, a reassuring sign to travellers in the dark. A life of goodness, Jesus suggested, shines in just the same open and unmistakable way.

No one, Jesus pointed out, lights a lamp and then covers it with a basket, for a lamp is set upon a stand so that it can give light to everyone in the house. In the same way, his followers were to let their good deeds be seen. The aim, he explained, was not to win praise for themselves but to lead others to give glory to their Father in heaven.

Jesus then reassured his listeners that he had not come to abolish the Law and the Prophets, the sacred writings of his people, but to fulfil them. Heaven and earth might pass away, he said, before the smallest letter of the Law was lost. His teaching, in other words, was offered as the completion of a long tradition and not as a break with it.

Jesus warned that his followers' goodness must surpass that of the scribes and Pharisees, the respected religious teachers of his day. The remark was not meant as a general insult, and what follows shows what he had in mind. Obeying the rules on the outside, he suggests, is not enough if the heart is left untouched.

Jesus reminded his listeners that the old law had said, “You shall not murder.” Then he pressed the commandment further, teaching that the roots of violence lie in anger and contempt, and that insulting another person is a serious matter in its own right. By moving from the deed to the feeling behind it, he turned a rule about actions into a lesson about character.

If you are bringing a gift to the altar, Jesus said, and you remember that someone has a grievance against you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled with that person, and only then come back to make your offering. Worship, he implied, is hollow when it is offered alongside an unmended quarrel, and a gift means little if it is given with a hard heart.

Jesus advised his listeners to come to terms quickly with anyone who had a complaint against them, before the matter reached a judge. Otherwise, he warned, the quarrel might end in court and the offender in prison, where the debt would have to be paid to the last coin. The counsel is as practical as it is moral, for a small dispute settled early is far cheaper than a large one fought late.

Jesus taught that faithfulness to a husband or wife is not merely a matter of what one does, since even a longing look begins to break the promise made in marriage. He used startling language about cutting off a hand or removing an eye, which most readers understand as deliberate exaggeration meant to show how seriously the matter should be taken. The point, as always in this sermon, is that goodness has to begin in the heart.

Jesus spoke about divorce as well, and he taught that marriage is a promise that must not be broken lightly. Christians have understood and applied this saying in different ways, and the traditions that treat it as binding and those that allow for exceptions each point to the text. What all agree upon is that Jesus held faithfulness in marriage to be a matter of great weight.

Jesus told his listeners not to make solemn promises by swearing oaths, whether by heaven, by the earth, or by their own heads, since none of these belongs to them. A plain “yes” or a plain “no,” he said, should be enough, and anything beyond it comes from the habit of deceit. The ideal he describes is a person whose word is so reliable that no oath is ever needed to support it.

The old law had said “an eye for an eye,” a rule designed to limit revenge to a fair measure and no more. Jesus went further and told his followers not to answer evil with evil, and that if someone strikes them on the cheek, they should turn the other as well. Scholars still debate how far he meant this literally, but its spirit, a refusal to be pulled into the cycle of retaliation, has inspired readers for centuries.

Jesus said to give to anyone who asks and not to turn away a person who wishes to borrow. If someone forces you to walk one mile, he added, go with that person for two, a saying that probably reminded his hearers of Roman soldiers, who could demand help from local people. Freely given service, he suggested, turns a burden that has been forced upon us into a gift that we choose to offer.

You have heard that it was said, “Love your neighbour and hate your enemy,” said Jesus, but I tell you to love your enemies and to pray for those who persecute you. This was one of the most demanding sayings of the whole sermon, and it remains so today. It asks the listener to wish good for the very people who have wished harm.

Your Father in heaven, Jesus said, makes his sun rise on the evil and the good alike and sends his rain on the just and the unjust. If you love only those who love you, he asked, what reward can you expect, since even tax collectors do as much? His followers were to be complete in goodness as their heavenly Father is complete, a word that many translations render as perfect.

When you give to the poor, Jesus said, do not announce it with trumpets, as hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets in order to be honoured by others. Give so privately that your left hand does not know what your right hand is doing. The reward of such giving, he said, comes from the Father who sees what is done in secret.

Do not pray like those who love to stand on the street corners to be seen, said Jesus. Go into your room, close the door, and pray to your Father in private, and do not heap up empty words, since God knows what you need before you ask. Prayer, in this teaching, is a quiet conversation with a loving Father and not a performance meant for an audience.

Jesus then taught his followers a short prayer that Christians now call the Lord's Prayer, and it has been said by countless people ever since. It asks that God's name be honoured and his kingdom come, and it asks for daily bread, for forgiveness, and for protection from evil. It begins with the words “Our Father in heaven,” which are among the most familiar in the world.

Jesus added a remark about forgiveness that follows the prayer, saying that if people forgive others when they do wrong, their heavenly Father will forgive them as well. If they refuse to forgive, he said, they should not expect to be forgiven themselves. The saying joins two things that most people prefer to keep apart, the mercy they hope to receive and the mercy they are willing to give.

When you fast, said Jesus, do not look gloomy as the hypocrites do, disfiguring their faces to show other people how serious they are. Anoint your head and wash your face, so that only your Father, who sees in secret, knows what you are doing. A discipline practised for show, he implied, has already received its reward in the admiration of the audience.

Do not store up for yourselves treasures on earth, said Jesus, where moths and rust destroy and thieves break in and steal. Store up treasures in heaven instead, where nothing can be lost or taken away. For where your treasure lies, he said, there your heart will also be found, so what we value most quietly shapes what we become.

The eye is the lamp of the body, said Jesus, so if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if it is unhealthy, your whole body will be full of darkness. Readers have usually taken this as a saying about how we look at life and what we allow ourselves to dwell upon. If the very light within us is darkened, he asks, how great is that darkness.

No one can serve two masters, said Jesus, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and money, he said, since each makes a claim on the whole of a person's loyalty. The sentence does not condemn wealth as such, but it insists that a person cannot be ruled by two opposite loyalties at once.

Jesus told his listeners not to worry about what they would eat or drink or wear, since life is more than food and the body more than clothes. Look at the birds of the air, he said, which neither plant nor harvest nor store food in barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not, he asked, worth far more to your Father than the birds that fly above your heads?

Why do you worry about clothes, asked Jesus, when you can look at the wild flowers growing in the fields, which neither work nor spin? Even King Solomon, in all his splendour, was not dressed as finely as one of these. If God clothes the grass of the field so beautifully, he said, will he not much more care for you?

Seek first the kingdom of God and his goodness, said Jesus, and all these other things will be given to you as well. So do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself, and each day has enough trouble of its own. It is a calm and practical piece of advice, and readers who are anxious by nature have returned to it again and again.

Do not judge, said Jesus, or you too will be judged, for in the same way that you judge others, you will be judged yourself. The measure you use for others, he said, will be the measure that is used for you in return, whether the judge is a neighbour or God. The saying does not forbid us to tell right from wrong, but it warns us against a habit of harshness that we would never wish to meet in return.

Why do you notice the speck of sawdust in your friend's eye, Jesus asked, and fail to see the log in your own? First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly enough to remove the speck from your friend's. The humour of the picture, an enormous plank in one eye, makes its lesson about self-honesty impossible to forget.

Do not give what is holy to dogs, said Jesus, and do not throw your pearls to pigs, or they may trample them and then turn and attack you. Readers have long understood this as a call to use wisdom about what is shared and with whom, since not every listener is ready to receive the deepest truths. It is one of the more puzzling lines in the sermon, and teachers have explained it in several ways.

Ask, and it will be given to you, said Jesus, seek, and you will find, and knock, and the door will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks the door will be opened. The saying is an invitation to persistence, and it describes a world in which the one who calls is not ignored.

Which of you, asked Jesus, if his son asked for bread, would give him a stone, or if he asked for a fish, would give him a snake? If you, imperfect as you are, know how to give good gifts to your children, he said, how much more will your Father in heaven give good things to those who ask him. The argument moves from the familiar love of a human parent to the far greater generosity of God.

In everything, Jesus said, do to others what you would want them to do to you, for this sums up the Law and the Prophets. Similar sayings, often called the Golden Rule, appear in many moral traditions of the world, but this version is notable for being put in a positive form. It asks not only that we avoid harm but that we actively do good.

Jesus told his listeners to enter by the narrow gate, for wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction, and many go through it. Small is the gate and narrow the road that leads to life, and only a few find it. The warning is not that the good life is closed to most people, but that it takes more attention and effort than drifting with the crowd.

Beware of false prophets, Jesus warned, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are hungry wolves. A gentle appearance, he implied, is easy to put on and difficult to keep, and a teacher's true character will in time be revealed. He asked his listeners to be watchful without being suspicious, which is a fine balance to strike.

You will recognise them by their fruit, said Jesus, for a good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not produce good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. The test he proposes is a practical one, since a person's real nature is shown less by what they say than by what they do over time.

Not everyone who says “Lord, Lord” to me, said Jesus, will enter the kingdom of heaven, but only the person who does the will of my Father. On the last day, he said, many will claim to have done great things in his name and will be told that he never knew them. The words are a sober warning that pious language, unaccompanied by a transformed life, is of no account.

Jesus ended the sermon with a story about two builders, which has remained one of the most famous parables in the Gospels. Everyone who hears these words of mine and puts them into practice, he said, is like a wise man who built his house on rock. The storm, when it came, would test the foundations rather than the decoration, and only what was truly sound would remain standing.

The rain came down, the rivers rose, and the winds beat against that house, yet it did not fall, because its foundation was on the rock. But the person who hears these words and does not act upon them, said Jesus, is like a foolish man who built his house on sand, and when the storm came, it fell with a great crash. The contrast could hardly be plainer, and it leaves the listener with a choice.

When Jesus had finished saying these things, Matthew tells us, the crowds were amazed at his teaching. He had taught them as one who had authority, and not as their teachers of the law, and it was clear that something new had been said on that hillside. The people who heard him did not forget it, and many of them followed him down the slope.

When Jesus came down from the mountain, large crowds followed him, and the Gospel moves on to the next story. The sermon itself has been read and discussed for about two thousand years, and Christians and many others have found in it a call to humility, mercy, honesty and trust. Its words are still being quoted today, and its simple images of salt, light, birds, flowers and a house on rock continue to speak to readers of every background.
